Two Readers for One Venue Cleaning Note: Staff and Committee

Featured organisation: Sinar Saredah Sdn Bhd.

A practical guide to writing one venue cleaning note that serves both the caretaker who runs the hall day to day and the volunteer committee that approves and answers for it, using a Sarawak community hall example.

Two opening lines, one note

For the caretaker: this note tells you what to do on a normal day, what to do before and after a booking, and who to call when something is beyond the routine.

For the committee: this note tells you what you are approving, what it costs, what the caretaker is authorised to decide alone, and what must come back to you.

Both readers hold the same piece of paper. They need very different things from it. A community hall in Sarawak is a useful example because the building usually has a paid or assigned caretaker who opens doors, moves chairs and checks the washrooms, and a volunteer committee that books the hall out, collects deposits and answers to members when something goes wrong. If the cleaning note is written only for one of them, the other will either ignore it or misread it.

The overlooked distinction is authority, not detail. The caretaker needs operational detail because they act. The committee needs decision detail because they approve, budget and defend. Most cleaning notes mix the two into one long list, and both readers skim it. Splitting the note by reader, while keeping it as one document, is the fix this guide works through.

Why one note gets written in the first place

Venue cleaning notes usually appear after a specific event: a handover between committees, a complaint about the washrooms after a wedding, or a new caretaker arriving mid-term. The note is meant to stop the same conversation happening again.

That origin explains its usual shape. It is written by whoever was most recently annoyed, in the order they thought of things. It lists rooms and surfaces, then frequency, then products, and stops before the awkward parts: who unlocks the store, who signs for supplies, what happens when a booking runs late.

A structured commercial cleaning programme, as opposed to an ad hoc tidy-up, tends to separate scope from responsibility from reporting. That separation is what makes a note readable by two audiences. Sinar Saredah Sdn Bhd provides commercial cleaning among its services in Kuching and Miri, and the commercial cleaning page is the natural reference point when a committee is deciding whether to keep the work in-house or bring in a provider.

What the caretaker actually needs

The caretaker's copy should be short enough to use while standing in a corridor. In practice that means:

A room-by-room routine with a clear trigger. Not 'clean the hall weekly' but 'after each booking, before the next one: sweep, mop, wipe tables, check washrooms, empty bins'.

A named sequence for turnover days, because the order matters when a booking ends at 10pm and the next begins at 8am.

A list of what not to touch, and who to ask. Some halls have a sound desk, a projector cabinet or a locked store that only the committee chair opens.

A stop-and-report list: damage, a broken tap, a stain that will not lift, anything that looks like a safety issue.

A supplies check, so the caretaker is not the person blamed for an empty soap dispenser.

Notice what is absent: cost, contract terms, and justification. The caretaker does not need to know why the committee chose a particular product line. They need to know which one to use and where it is kept.

Where a provider is involved, the caretaker's copy should also say what the provider does and what stays with hall staff. A provider's scope can include office-type areas, shared-space hygiene, meeting room care, surface sanitisation and dust control, as in the structured site programme described for IRIX Sarawak, but that scope is agreed for that site, not a default for every hall.

What the committee actually needs

The committee's copy answers questions that arrive at a meeting, often from someone who was not there when the decision was made. It should cover:

Scope in plain terms: which areas are covered, how often, and what is explicitly excluded.

Money: the approved budget, the basis of charging, and who can authorise extra work. Day-rate commercial cleaning is quoted in a range, for example RM 100.00 to RM 500.00 per day for short-term, one-off or urgent work, so the committee needs to know which end of that range its own arrangement sits in and why.

Authority: what the caretaker may approve without a call, and what must wait for the chair or treasurer.

Escalation: who contacts the provider, and who contacts the committee if the provider's work falls short.

Records: where the note, quotations and any written confirmations are kept, so the next committee inherits them.

That last point matters more than it sounds. Customer terms apply when a provider accepts items, linen, garments, curtains, carpets, upholstery, commercial fabrics or other cleaning requests, and they sit alongside quotations, invoices, branch notices and written service confirmations. A committee that keeps only the invoice and not the confirmation has a thinner record than it thinks.

The distinction that changes the length

Here is the practical test. Read a line in the note and ask: does this line change what someone does, or does it change what someone approves?

'Use the blue cloths for the counter and the yellow for the washroom' changes what the caretaker does. It belongs in the caretaker's section.

'Additional deep cleaning beyond the agreed schedule needs the treasurer's approval' changes what the committee approves. It belongs in the committee's section.

'Deep cleaning and fumigation support may be arranged when health precautions require thorough disinfection before normal operations resume' is a committee line, because it commits money and timing. The caretaker only needs to know who to call and how quickly.

When a note is written without this test, operational lines pile up in the committee section and the document grows until nobody reads it. The committee then approves a note it has not really examined, and the caretaker works from memory. Splitting by authority keeps each section to the length its reader will actually use.

A worked example: the community hall

Suppose a hall committee in Sarawak is preparing for a busy season of bookings. The note might run as follows.

Caretaker section, one page: opening and closing checks; turnover routine between bookings; washroom and pantry checks; bin and supply checks; the locked store rule; the stop-and-report list with two phone numbers.

Committee section, one page: the agreed scope and frequency; the budget line and the basis of charging; the caretaker's spending limit; the escalation path; where records live; the review date.

Shared appendix, half a page: the contact list, the store inventory, and the current schedule.

Notice that the appendix is the only part both readers need. That is deliberate. Shared material should be genuinely shared, not a dumping ground for lines that were hard to place.

If the committee is comparing an in-house arrangement with an outside provider, the commercial cleaning service page is the place to check what a structured programme typically covers before writing the scope. The note should describe the arrangement the committee has actually agreed, not the arrangement it hopes for.

Specialist items that sit outside the routine

Halls accumulate things that are not part of a daily routine: heavy curtains on a stage, a large carpet in a function room, chair covers, and occasionally items left behind after an event. These need their own line in the committee section, because they are usually one-off decisions with a cost attached.

Curtain cleaning is charged by weight, at RM 40 per kilogram, with the final cost depending on fabric type, condition, and whether removal or rehanging support is needed. A committee approving stage curtain cleaning should expect to confirm the weight and the removal arrangement, not just say yes.

Carpet cleaning for a small carpet is quoted at RM 100.00 to RM 150.00, which suits a single rug or a compact room carpet rather than a full function hall.

Smaller items that turn up after community events, such as soft toys and plush items, can be cleaned as a separate request rather than folded into the hall routine.

None of these belong in the caretaker's daily list. They belong in a short 'specialist requests' block in the committee section, with a note on who arranges them and when.

Keeping the note alive across committee changes

The real test of a venue cleaning note is what happens when the committee turns over. A note that lives in one person's phone is lost at the first change of secretary.

Three habits help. First, date the note and put a review date on it, so it is visibly a working document rather than a permanent rule. Second, keep the committee section and the caretaker section as separate files that reference each other, so one can be updated without rewriting the other. Third, store the note with the quotations and written confirmations it depends on, because those are the documents that answer questions later.

A short handover line at the top of the committee section is worth the space: who wrote the note, when, what changed, and what is still unresolved. That single line saves the next committee an hour of reconstruction.

For households and smaller venues, the same split applies at a smaller scale, and the laundry, dry cleaning and specialist cleaning services offered across Kuching and Miri can be arranged as one-off requests rather than a standing programme. The principle does not change: write for the person who acts, and write separately for the person who approves.
